title: Poll: Plurality of Marylanders back the Birds rather than the Nationals
summary: Baseball is a game of stats and nothing says statistics like a good poll. In the third part of its latest poll, the UMBC Institute of Politics asked about baseball -- about 4 in 10 said they were Orioles fans -- news consumption and general political knowledge
content:
by Bryan P. Sears, Maryland Matters April 2, 2026

by Bryan P. Sears, Maryland Matters April 2, 2026

Nothing says baseball like a good poll.

And a new survey released Thursday by the University of Maryland, Baltimore County is pretty good if you are a fan of the Birds of Baltimore.

A plurality of Marylanders — 4 in 10 — identify as fans of the Baltimore Orioles, compared to just 16% who declared their devotion to the Washington Nationals.

“This feels like me. I think about that 40%, in all seriousness, really does capture the spectrum of fandom from the general affinity — the people who say, ‘I like the Bird’ — to people who are the die-hards,” said Mileah Kromer, director of the poll at the UMBC Institute of Politics. “And that’s where it starts. I think that you need that general affinity to get things started.”

The poll surveyed 804 Maryland adults between March 17 and 22. Of those, 731 identified as registered voters. The margin of error for the poll is 3.5%.

Part one of the poll, released Tuesday, covered the economy and affordability issues. Part two, released Wednesday, included new, lower job approval numbers for Gov. Wes Moore (D).

Roughly 9% told Kromer they cheer for “some other team.” One-third of those surveyed said they are “not really a baseball fan.”

Moore job approval falls below 50% for the first time

Full disclosure: Kromer is a season ticket holder at Camden Yards. But she assured Maryland Matters that she did not place an Orange-and-Black-stained thumb on the scale.

“I certainly didn’t put my thumb on the scale, but I certainly celebrate the response nonetheless,” Kromer said.

Kromer’s poll also asked Marylanders about where they are getting their news and tested the knowledge of those surveyed with a small pop quiz on Maryland state government.

Nearly two-thirds of people surveyed said they pay “a great deal” or at least “some” attention to news about state government and politics in any given week. About 35% said they pay “little” or “no attention at all.”

For those who said they paid at least a little attention, 67% said the biggest source of information on state government and politics is local television news programs.

Kromer said the public is flooded with information about budgets and the governor and elections every day.

Kromer, who is also a political science professor, gave a pop quiz — five multiple-choice questions, focused on facts news consumers would likely have run across watching, listening to or reading coverage of state government and politics issues.

Questions included the length of the term of office for Maryland’s governor. More than 6 in 10 answered correctly. Also included were questions about the length of the Maryland General Assembly legislative session or the approximate share of seats held by Democratic Party — which 29% and 21% got right, respectively.

The average respondent answered two of the five questions correctly. Roughly 19% of those surveyed correctly answered at least four of the five questions.

“But recalling factual information about politics is difficult for some folks,” she said. “It’s important to note, and this is something I actually, I sincerely believe, people aren’t that great at factual recall, but they still can make judgments on if things are good or bad, or who to vote for, based on what they encounter in their everyday life.”

Kromer’s poll did not contain any demographic information on Maryland Matters readers. But we suspect we know what those results would be.
